topic.title: Nasted If-Else Statement in C
topic.description: Conditional execution using if-else statements. Decision making and branching logic in C programs.

learningNotes.whatILearned: To find the largest of three, ask the first question — is `a` bigger than `b` — and only then ask the second.
learningNotes.challenges: I wrote the nesting correctly but never checked the numbers I read, so three missing answers print the highest of three random values.
learningNotes.nextSteps: Read the three numbers with one checked `scanf`, and put a comment on the nested `if` saying why the second question only matters when the first answer is yes.

misconceptions: `scanf` returns how many items it read — the value is only ever set if you check that, so a missing answer leaves the variable untouched
The nested `if` is only correct because the first branch already guarantees `a > b` — that is the reason the second comparison does not need `b` in it, and it is worth saying so
engine.review:
**The rubric I used**

There is no task sheet for this one — it was written before the engine
existed, so there was nothing to grade it against. I graded the file on the
three things that have always mattered here:

- **40 — it runs.** It compiles or interprets without an error.
- **30 — it is right.** The output is what it claims to produce.
- **30 — it explains itself.** Comments say *why*, not *what*.

**40 + 30 + 0 = 70%**

**What is solid**

The nesting is right, and this is the point of the exercise. The outer test asks whether `a` beats `b`; only if it does does the inner test compare `a` with `c`. When the outer test fails, the code already knows `a` is out, so it compares `b` with `c` and prints one of those. I ran it with 3, 5 and 9 and it printed `9 is the highest number among the 3 numbers.`

It compiles clean.

**What is not**

`scanf("%d%d%d", &a, &b, &c)` is not checked, so three missing answers give three meaningless comparisons. And there is no comment on the one thing that makes this code correct — that inside the first branch, `a > b` is already known, which is why the inner comparison only needs `c`.

**The one thing to fix first**

One comment on the inner `if`:

```c
/* We only get here when a > b, so only c can still be bigger. */
```

That single line is the difference between code that is correct and code that a reader can see is correct.
